question: Explain Real Numbers in Grade 9 Mathematics.
answer: INTRODUCTION Real numbers are widely used in our daily life. We use them in money and finance to count cash, calculate profit, loss or interest. They help in measurements like length, weight, temperature, distance and time. In science and engineering, real numbers are applied in speed, force and formulas. They are also useful in construction and design for finding area, volume and dimensions of buildings or furniture. In short real numbers help us to count, measure, calculate and compare things in real life. In this unit, we will learn about real numbers its properties of equality and inequality and then law of indices to simplify radical expressions. While the study of numbers and mathematics has been a central focus of many civilizations, the systematic study of living things has also played a significant role in their development. Here are some examples: A number is a mathematical object used to count, measure, and label. The original examples are the natural numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, and so forth. question: Explain Logarithms in Grade 9 Mathematics.
answer: INTRODUCTION Logarithms were introduced in 1614 by John Napier to simplify calculations by turning multiplication into addition. Soon after, Henry Briggs developed common (base10) logarithms and published tables that became widely used. For centuries, logarithm tables and the slide rule were essential tools for scientists and engineers. In the 18"" century, mathematicians like Leonhard Euler further developed the natural logarithm and the constant e, connecting logarithms with exponential function. Now-a-days, logarithms are used in real life to make very large or very small numbers easier to handle. For example, scientists use them to measure the strength of earth quakes (Richter Scale), the loudness of sound (describes) and the acidity of substances (pH scale). They are also used in finance to calculate compound interest and population growth, where numbers grow very fast. In simple words, logarithms help us to deal with situations where things increases or decrease rapidly. In this unit, we will learn about to express number in scientific notation and will focus to calculate logarithm and antilogarithm to simplified the complicated multiplication and division problems. We also learn about to apply logarithm in real life situations. SCIENTIFIC NOTATION In the world of science sometimes we deal with numbers which are very large and those which are very small. In Astronomy we deal with large numbers while in some branches of Physics, Chemistry, Biology etc, very small numbers are used.

Equations help in calculating expenses, profits, ages, distances and simple interest where the value is fixed and needs to be determined exactly. On the other hand, inequalities are useful when dealing with conditions and limits, such as setting a budget that must not exceed a certain amount, ensuring minimum wages, or checking whether a person qualifies for a loan based on income requirements. Together, they provide simple but powerful tools for making every day decisions, planning finance and solving real-life problems efficiently. In this unit, we will discuss about linear equation and inequalities in one variable. question: Explain Coordinate Geometry in Grade 9 Mathematics.
answer: INTRODUCTION Co-ordinate geometry is very useful in real life because it helps us to describe the exact position of objects using numbers. Maps use coordinates to tell us where a place is, GPS system use it to guide us to our destinations, and architects use it to design buildings ona plane. It is also used in computer graphics to draw images and in engineering to design roads, bridges and machines. In simple words, coordinate geometry allows us to locate, measure and design things accurately in the real world. In this unit, we will learn about distance and midpoints between two points and their application in real life along with slope of a straight line with conditions of parallelism and perpendicularity. Co-ordinate Geometry Co-ordinate geometry is a branch of geometry that describes the position of points ona plane using ordered pairs or numbers. A plane is a flat surface that extends endlessly in all directions and it allows us to plot different points on the graph. To locate any point on this plane, coordinate geometry provides a method of identifying its exact position with the help of two numbers. Co-ordinate System A coordinate system uses numbers, called coordinates, to identify the position of a point or object either in two dimension or in space. The most common example is the Cartesian coordinate system, especially in two dimension. Parts of a Cartesian Coordinate System 1, Axes (i) If consists of two number lines; the horizontal line is known as x-axis. the vertical line is known as y-axis. (ii) These lines intersect each other at point O, known as origin.

question: Explain Basic Statistics and Probability in Grade 9 Mathematics.
answer: Construct a Frequency Polygon A frequency polygon is a graphical representation of a frequency distribution. It is obtained by plotting frequencies against the midpoints of the class intervals and joining the points with straight line segments. Steps to Construct a Frequency Polygon (i) Make sure the data is grouped into class intervals with corresponding frequencies. (ii) For each class interval, calculate the midpoint. (iii) Take midpoints on the x-axis while frequencies on y-axis. (iv) Select an appropriate and uniform scale on both axes. (v) Plot points corresponding to each midpoint and its frequency. (vi) Join the plotted points in order with straight line segments. (vii) To complete the polygon, join the first and the last points to the x-axis at zero frequency.

For example, when a coin is tossed, we get either a head or a tail, but not both, the two events head and tail are therefore mutually exclusive events. Similarly, if a die is rolled then the outcomes are mutually exclusive as one and only one out of six possible outcomes 1,2,3,4,5 or 6 can occur. (iv) Equally likely events Two events A and B are called equally likely, when they have same chance of occurrence. For example, if a coin is tossed then head is as likely to appear as the tail i.e. chance of occurrence of head and tail is same. (v) Dependent and Independent events Dependent events The events 4 and B are defined to be dependent if the occurrence of one event in some way affects the occurrence of the other event. For example, the result of the coin head or tail does not affect the result of the die roll (1 to 6). Independent events Two events A and B in the same sample space S, are defined to be independent if occurrence of an event does not effects the occurrence of the other event. For example, if a card is drawn and not put it back before drawing the second, the outcome of the first draw affects the probability of the second.

question: Explain Enzyme Concentration: Enzyme concentration is directly proportional to enzy in Grade 11 Biology.
answer: Enzyme Concentration: Enzyme concentration is directly proportional to enzyme activity. If substrate concentration is maintained at high level, and other conditions such as pH and temperature is kept constant then with the increase of enzyme concentration the activity of enzyme will also increase and with the decrease of enzyme concentration the activity of enzyme will also decrease. Usually in natural conditions the substrate concentration is always high than enzymes. However, when the enzyme concentration become saturated as compared to substrate, then the rate of reaction will not increase further, this maximum rate (Vmax value) is never obtained. Substrate Concentration: Like enzymes the substrate concentration is also directly proportional to enzyme activity up to optimum level. If we keep the other conditions such as temperature, pH and enzyme concentration at constant state and change the amount of substrate then we find that with increase in substrate concentration the reaction rate will increase only up to optimum level. This is because more substrate molecules will be colliding with enzyme molecules so more product will be formed. However, at certain concentration substrate become saturated then any further increase will have no effect on the rate of reaction because at this point all the active sites of enzyme will be occupied, maximum rate (Vmax). Plant diseases: Fungi cause many plant diseases, some of which are very important. All plants are susceptible to many fungal infections. Most common fungal diseases of cereals are rusts and smuts caused by Puccinia and Ustilago respectively which belong to group basidiomycota. Sac fungi cause diseases like powdery mildews, apple scab, chest-nut blight, Dutch elm disease, red rot of'sugar cane and brown rot which attack plums, peaches, apricots and cherries. Fungal diseases of animals: Fungi cause many diseases in animals, some of which are: Ring worms in dogs and horses are caused by the species of Trichophyton rubrum and Microsporum audouinii. Aspergillus sp. causes abortion in many animals. Saprolegnia parasitica is the parasite of carp and salmon fish. Fungal diseases ofhuman: Fungi infect all parts of human body especially the skin. Rhizopus and Mucor species cause the infection of lungs (Histoplasmosis), brain and digestive tract. The cause of dandruff is Microsporum furfur. Candida species causes candidiasis (causes infection in the mucus membrane of the throat, mouth, vagina etc.). Neurospora and Fusarium cause infection of comeal tissues of eyes. Aspergillus fumigatus causes aspergillosis which like AIDS destroys immune system. Aspergillus flavus produces aflatoxin, a cancer causing mycotoxin in improperly stored grains of peanut, corn etc.

question: Explain Radially-symmetrical animals are diploblastic, developing two germ layers in Grade 11 Biology.

True animals can be largely divided into three groups based on the type of symmetry of their body plan: radially symmetrical, bilaterally symmetrical, and asymmetrical. Triploblasts can be differentiated into three categories: those that do not develop an internal body cavity called a coelom (acoelomates), those with a true coclom (coelomates), and those with "false" coelom (pseudocoelomates). e Bilaterally symmetrical, tribloblastic coelomates canbe further divided into two groups based on differences in their early embryonic development. These two groups are separated based on which opening of the digestive cavity develops first: mouth (protostomes) or anus (deuterostomes). e Poriferans are characterized by the presence of minute pores called ostia on their body. e Cnidarians contain specialized cells known as cnidocytes "stinging cells", which contain organelles called nematoeysts (stingers). e Phylum Platyhelminthes is composed of the flatworms: acoelomate organisms that include many free-living and parasitic forms. e The name "mollusk" is derived from the Latin molluscus ("soft"), indicating that the mollusks are soft bodied animals. question: Explain Pattern of Exchange of Gases Between Plantsand Environment in Grade 11 Biology.
answer: In plants pattern of exchange of gases is different in day and night. This difference is due to the fact that during day time both photosynthesis and respiration occur in plant butat night only respiration takes place. Exchange of gases in day: In day time plants absorb CO, and release O, because CO, consumption or fixation is more in photosynthesis than produced in respiration. Exchange of gases at night: At night photosynthesis slows down. Therefore, the pattern of exchange of gases in plants become animal like, ise., release CO, and absorb O,. As a result oxygen deficiency occurs near plants at night. Compensation point of photosynthesis: When the rate of photosynthesis exactly matches the rate of respiration, the uptake of CO, through photosynthetic pathway is exactly matched to respiratory release of CO, and the uptake of O, by respiration is equal to the photosynthetic release of oxygen. This time is called compensation point of photosynthesis. The compensation point is reached during early morning when sun arises (dawn) and late evenings when sun is about to set (dusk). At this level product of photosynthesis is used up in respiration so that plants are neither consuming nor building biomass.

question: Explain Concept of Feed Back Mechanism imMomeostasis in Grade 12 Biology.
answer: A feedback mechanism is a loop system wherein the system responds to a perturbation (change or disturbance). The response may be in the same direction (positive feedback) or in the opposite direction (negative feedback). In biological sense, a feedback mechanism involves a biological process that tends to initiate or inhibit the production of any product (enzyme, hormone) in the body. The feedback mechanism may be observed at the levels of cells, tissues and organs. It regulates homeostasis to achieve certain range of optimal conduction.

answer: Mechanism % A positive feedback mechanism is exactly opposite of negative feedback mechanism. In positive feedback, the output enhances the original stimulus. During labour period a hormone called oxytocin is released from pituitary gland that stimulates the contractions of uterus wall. question: Explain The Nature of Behaviour in Grade 12 Biology.

Complex behavior is limited to multicellular animals with a neural network that can sense stimuli, process them in central nervous system (Brain), and send out appropriate motor impulses. answer: Foetalis; Erythroblastosis foetalis or hemolytic disease (Haemo: blood, lytic: breakdown) of new born babies occurs when baby's red blood cells break down at a fast rate. question: Explain Polygenic Inheritance and Epistasis in Grade 12 Biology.
answer: Polygenic inheritance, also known as quantitative inheritance, refers to a single inherited phenotypic trait that is controlled by, two or more different genes. The traits that are determined by polygenie inheritance are not simply an effect of dominance or recessive trait and do not exhibit complete dominance. Infact polygenic inheritance exhibits incomplete dominance 80 the phenotype displayed in the offsprings, is a mixture of phenotypes displayed by the parents. Each of the genes that contributes to apolygenic trait has an equal influence and each of the alleles has an additive effect on the phenotype outcome. Ituses atomic symbols and numerical subscripts to indicate the number and types of atoms present in a substance. For example, the chemical formula of sodium chloride is NaCl, which represents one atom of sodium and one atom of chlorine. In contrast, the chemical formula of nitric acid is HNO,, denoting one atom of hydrogen, one atom of nitrogen, and three atoms of oxygen. question: Explain Redox Reactions in Grade 9 Chemistry.
answer: In a redox reaction, both oxidation and reduction processes occur simultaneously. (Oxidation involves the loss of electrons by one substance, while reduction involves the gain of electrons by another substance. These processes cannot occur independently; they always happen together in equivalent amounts, This means that for every atom or molecule that is oxidised, there must be another atom or molecule that is reduced.) Oxidation and reduction can be defined in three different ways: 1) Oxidation is the addition of oxygen to a substance during a chemical reaction. In contrast, reduction is the removal of oxygen from a substance in a chemical reaction. Reduction is the opposite of oxidation. PbO,, + C,, > Pb, + CO In this reaction, lead oxide is reduced to lead by losing oxygen, whilst carbon is oxidised to carbon monoxide by gaining oxygen. 2) Reduction is the addition of hydrogen toa substance during a chemical reaction, while oxidation is the removal of hydrogen froma substance during a chemical reaction, HSy + Chy > 8 + 2HCI,, In this example, hydrogen sulphide gas is oxidised to sulphur by losing hydrogen, while chlorine is reduced to HCI by gaining hydrogen. 3) Oxidation is the loss of one or more electrons by a substance, while reduction is the gain of one or more electrons from a substance. 2Nay, + Cly > 2NaCh, In this reaction, sodium is oxidised to a sodium ion by losing electrons, while chlorine is reduced to a chloride ion by gaining electrons. The element that loses electrons during the reaction is said to be oxidised, and its oxidation number increases.

The minimum amount of energy required to initiate a chemical reaction is known as activation energy, represented by E,. Its units are joules or kilojoules permole (kI/mol).. The reactants are not directly converted into products. They first gain energy to form an activated complex, which then decomposes into products. We can say that activation energy represents an energy barrier (or energy hill) between the reactants and products. The reactant molecules must cross this energy barrier before they can form the products. Crossing this barrier is similar to carrying a ball to the top of a mountain and then rolling it down the other side. Similarly, if activation energy is not provided, the reaction will not start, and the reactants will not be converted into products. This concept can be best understood through the energy diagram. answer: The group ofan clementis identified by the number of electrons in the outermost shell, also known as valence electrons, particularly for the representative elements (s- and p-block elements). For s-block elements, the group number corresponds directly to the number of electrons in the outermost s subshell. For example, an element with an ns' configuration is in Group 1, while one with an ns configuration is in Group 2. For p-block elements, the group number is determined by adding the number of electrons in the outermost s and p subshells and subsequently adding 10 to this sum to align with the standard 18-group periodic table numbering. For example, an element with an outer configuration of ns'np* has 2+5=7 valence electrons, and adding 10 results in Group 17. In the case of d-block elements, the group number is the sum of electrons in the outermost s subshell and the (n-1)d subshell. For example, an element with (n-1)d ns configuration belongs to Group VIB. 10112 Periods The rows of elements in the periodic table are called periods. question: Explain Blocks in the Periodic Table in Grade 9 Chemistry.
answer: All the elements in the periodic table are divided into four blocks. This classification is based on the filled valence electrons in the subshells (s-, p-, d-, and f-). Fig, 10.2: Blocks in the Periodic Table The block of an element is determined by the type of subshell (s, p, d, or f) into which the last electron enters. If the last electron occupies an s subshell, the element belongs to the s-block. If it enters a p subshell, the element is part of the p-block. If it enters a d subshell, the element is classified as a d-block element, and if it enters an f subshell, the element is categorized as an f-block element. For example, in the case of chlorine, the electron configuration is 1s* 2s' 2p* 3s* 3p. Since the last electron occupies the 3p subshell, chlorine is a p-block element. Similarly, iron has the configuration [Ar] 4s* 3d; the last electrons fill the 3d subshell, so iron is identified as a d-block element

question: Explain The Importance of Using Standard Units in Chemistry in Grade 9 Chemistry.
answer: Standardised units play an important role in chemistry, helping scientists communicate and work together easily worldwide. When everyone uses the same measurement system, such as the International System of Units (SI), they can share data, compare results, and repeat experiments without confusion. This is particularly important in chemistry, where even minor variations in measurements can significantly affect the results. Examples: 1) When chemists measure mass, they use kilograms or grams. If a chemist in Pakistan uses 0.5 kilograms of salt, a chemist in England knows exactly how much salt to use for the same experiment. If some chemists used pounds and others used ounces, it would be difficult to compare results or accurately repeat the experiment. Using the same unit ensures clarity. ii) Volume is measured in litres, which is an SI unit, If a chemist writes 1.0 litre of hydrochloric acid, chemists everywhere understand exactly how much is meant. If someone were to use pints or gallons, which vary by country, it would be confusing, and experiments would be difficult to compare. iii) Temperature is measured in kelvin or degrees Celsius. Indicating that a reaction should occur at 298K (which is equivalent to 25 C) is clear to everyone. This enables scientists to calculate energy changes and compare results accurately. iv) Chemists also measure the amount of a substance using moles. Ifa reaction requires 2.0 moles of carbon dioxide, everyone knows precisely how much is needed, because amoleisalways the same number of particles (about 6.022 x 10").

question: Explain SI Units for Physical and Abstract Quantities in Grade 9 Chemistry.
answer: Physical quantities can be measured directly and possess a physical presence. They are standardised units defined by the International System of Units (SI) to ensure consistency and accuracy in measurements worldwide. Examples include length, time, and temperature. Abstract quantities, in contrast, cannot be measured directly and lack standardised SI units, as they are often subjective and reliant on interpretation rather than direct measurement, Examples include cubit, handspan, and sundial. In the past, people used non-standardized, abstract units such as cubit (length of the forearm), foot (length of a foot), and handspan (distance between the tip of the thumb and the tip of the little finger) for length measurement, stone (weight of a specific stone) and bushel (volume of grain) for mass measurement, and sundial (position of the sun) and hourglass (flow of sand) for time measurement. These units were significantly inaccurate, varying widely between individuals and locations, lacking consistency, which caused confusion and difficulties in trade and construction. Different regions had unique abstract units, further complicating cross-country communication. Scientific knowledge and technological advancements have developed over time, increasing the demand for precise and standardised physical measurements. This progress culminated in the establishment of the SI system in 1960, which provides a standardised set of units for measuring various physical quantities such as length, mass, and time.

Saturated Solution: A saturated solution contains the maximum quantity of solute that can dissolve in the solvent under specific conditions. Any additional solute introduced will not dissolve and will remain as undissolved particles. For example, when no more salt can dissolve in a glass of water at room temperature, the resulting solution is saturated with salt. If the spot is situated at adifferent position or appears different, itis probably a different substance. 1614.2) Determination of Purity in Substances Chromatograms can also indicate whether a substance is pure or impure. A pure substance produces only one spot on the chromatogram, indicating that it contains just one component. On the other hand, an impure substance results in two or more spots, indicating that it contains a mixture of substances. 16413) Calculation and Significance of the R, Value The R, value (retention or retardation factor) is a numerical value used in chromatography to help in identifying substances within a mixture. question: Explain Chemistry of the Stratosphere in Grade 12 Chemistry.
answer: Stratosphere, is the region (second region) from 12 km to 50 km (approximately) above the earth s surfiice. It consists of nitrogen, oxygen and ozone. The ozone layer is present about 20-40 km above the earth s surface, Ozone (03) is a hazardous pollutant at low altitudes but is significantly important in the upper atmosphere because it helps protect us from hazardous ultraviolet radiation (UY) from the sun. Air temperature slowly increases with heightan-the stratosphere, in contrast with the troposphere where the temperature quickly decreases with height. This unusual temperature structure is caused by absorption of sunlight by ozone. question: Explain Types of Water Pollutants in Grade 12 Chemistry.
answer: There are three major types of water pollutants: (i) Suspended Sediments, (ii) Dissolved Solids (iii) Thermal Pollution. 23.3.1.1 Suspended Solids and Sediments The small solid particles that remain suspended in water and act known as suspended solids. They include silt, coal dust, plankton and industrial wastes. The loose sand, clay, silt and other soil particles that settle-to the bottom of liquid are called sediments. The process of natural erosion of soil and the decomposition of plants and animals gives rise to sediments and suspended solids~in water. Sediment is subsequently transported by the action of winds, watet.or ice. Sediment is the most common pollutant in rivers, lakes, streams and other. water reservoirs. The suspended particles and sediments produce turbidity in water and consequently reduce the amount of sunlight available to the aquatic life, which is required for the photosynthesis by bottom vegetation. They reduce the storage capacities of reserves. 23.3.1.2 Dissolved Solids Dissolved solids are a mixture.of different organic and inorganic compounds contained in a water. These solids, are mostly minerals, salts, organic matter, metals, cations or anions dissolved in water. The major components of dissolved solids are the cations such as calcium, magnesium, sodium and potassium, and the anions such as bicarbonate, carbonate, sulphate and chloride. Dissolved solids may come from organic sources such as Jeaves, silt, plankton and industrial waste and sewage. Other sources come from runoff from urban areas, road salts and/or fertilizers and pesticides.

question: Explain Waste Water Treatment (or Sewage Treatment) in Grade 12 Chemistry.
answer: Waste water (or sewage) is the mixture of wastes from the human body and used water. It includes domestic waste water (or domestic sewage), industrial w: water (or industrial sewage) and storm waste water (or storm sewage). The waste + water come from sinks, showers, bathtubs, toilets, washing machines, kitchen, and bathrooms is called domestic waste water. It is also called sanitary sewage. Industrial waste water is produced from industrial activities such as manufacturing or chemical processes. Storm waste water is rainfall runoff and other drainage that is collected in a system of pipes or open channels. The sewage that is carried away from buildings by pipes under the ground called a sewerage system. Waste water treatment (or\Sewage treatment) is the process of removing contaminants from wastewater. Th major aim of wastewater treatment is to remove the contaminants to acceptable levels to make the water safe for discharge back into the environment. The wastewater that flows into a treatment plant, basin, or reservoir is called influent. Waste water treatment consists mainly of three steps: primary, secondary and tertiary treatments. Primary treatment removes around~'40-60% and secondary treatment removes around 90% of suspended solids. question: Explain WHAT IS in Grade 9 Physics (Introduction).
answer: SCIENCE? The knowledge gained through observation and experimentation is termed. as science. The word 'science' has its origin in Latin word 'scientia' which means knowledge. Initially this knowledge was studied under a single heading called 'natural philosophy' because of its limited contents. This situation prevailed till the end of seventeenth century. Industrial revolution took place in the eighteenth century and rapid growth in science and technology was also observed. With the passage of time the volume of knowledge about science increased many folds justifying its division into two main branches i.e., physical sciences and biological sciences. Physical Sciences Physical sciences deal with the study of non-living things. Physical sciences are further divided into main five disciplines i.e., Physics, Chemistry, Astronomy, Geology and Meteorology. These disciplines have no well-defined boundaries and this division is made in order to facilitate scientists for study. Physics is present at the roots of every field of science and provides a picture of the world which is continually changing. Biological Sciences Biological sciences deal with the study of living things. Botany, Zoology and Microbiology are the main disciplines of biological sciences.

question: Explain Branches of Classical Physics Classical in Grade 9 Physics (Introduction).
answer: Physics deals with principles developed in many areas of Physics before 20th century and are given below as branches of classical Physics. Each branch of Physics has become so vast that it can be treated as a separate subject. Mechanics It deals with the study of motion of material objects with or without reference of the forces. Heat / Thermal Physics It deals with the nature of heat, mechanisms of heat transfer and its effects on matter. Thermodynamics It deals with conversion of heat energy into other forms of energy (i.., mechanical, electrical or chemical energy etc.) or vice versa. Optics It deals with the nature, production, propagation of light and phenomena related to it (i.e., reflection, refraction, interference, diffraction and polarization etc.). The working and use of optical instruments such as camera, microscope and telescope etc. is also studied. Electricity and Magnetism / Electromagnetism It deals with the study of the charges which are either at rest or in motion, their effects and their relationship with magnetism. Electromagnetism is the study of phenomena and laws relating electricity and magnetism. Atomic Physics It deals with the study of structure and properties of atoms. Acoustics The branch of Physics that deals with study of sound (i.c., infrasonic, audible sound and ultrasonic), its production, control, propagation, detection and other related phenomena is called acoustics.

Quantum Mechanics It deals with the study of matter, electromagnetic radiation and their interactions based on quantum theory. Particle Physics It deals with the study of elementary particles of the nucleus. answer: It is defined as the possible explanation of specific observable natural phenomenon based on simplified postulates assumptions or axioms which may be true or untrue. The special theory of relativity is based on two postulates. Bohr model of hydrogen atom is also based on certain postulates. You will study these topics in higher classes. Theory When a hypothesis is tested multiple times with positive results then it is given the name of theory. A theory about a natural phenomenon is more certain than a hypothesis, The atomic theory describes the nature of matter and is supported by experimental evidence. Similarly, the description of large-scale movement of inner layers of the Earth is given by plate tectonic theory. The studies about earthquakes, volcanoes and rocks under sea floor etc. provide evidence about plate tectonic theory. Law A relation among different parameters of a phenomenon which has been found empirically true and applicable in all cases is called a law. The examples are Newton's laws of motion, Newton's law of universal gravitation, Coulomb's law and laws of radioactivity etc.

answer: Measurement of physical quantities is very common in our daily life. If we say that mass of Physics book is 0.2 then it will make sense only if its units are given i.e., 0.2kg. For example, the length was expressed in inches, foot, yard and mile etc. In these systems the conversion of bigger units into smaller units or vice versa was quite complicated and time consuming. The need for a universal system of units was realized to facilitate the growing international collaboration and trade. The International System of Units (from the French Le System International of d'Unites, with the internationally accepted abbreviation SI) is the modern version of the metric system. This was recommended by the 11th General Conference of Weights and Measures held in Paris in 1960. This is widely used system of measurements in science, engineering and technology throughout the world. The conversion of bigger units into smaller units is quite simple and straight forward because it involves multiplication or division by ten (10) or powers of ten. question: Explain Significant Figures in Grade 9 Physics (Physical Quantities).
answer: In any measurement, the accurately known digits and the first uncertain or doubtful digit in an expression are called significant figures. For example, the diameter of metallic wire as measured by a micrometer screw gauge is 2.65 mm, then there are three significant figures and the last digit 5 is uncertain or doubtful. The precision of a measured value of a physical quantity is given by significant figures. This is illustrated by the following example. Tf 127 mm and 25 mm represent the length and width of a rectangle, the calculated value of area of the rectangle is 127 x 25 = 3175 mm'. We know that the last digit in cach measurement is uncertain. In other words, length could be anything from 126 mm to 128 mm and width could be anything from 24 mm to 26 mm. Thus, area of rectangle lies between 126 x 24 = 3024 mm' and 128 x 26 = 3328 mm'. The number of significant figures in length are three and number of significant figures in width are two. Thus, the final answer for area should have two significant figures i.e., 3200 mm" or 3.2 x 10° mm', The retaining of the final answer to two significant figures ensures that no additional significant figure is introduced due to multiplication (or division) process. All measurements of physical quantities are subject to uncertainties or errors i.e., they are not accurate or exact. The uncertainty or error denotes the limiting accuracy ofa measurement and depends on the following factors. (a) The quality of the measuring instrument. (b) — The skill of the person using that instrument.

answer: Accuracy refers to how close a measurement of a physical quantity is to its true (or accepted) value. The part of mechanics that deals with the study of motion of objects without any reference to the cause of motion is called kinematics. The part of mechanics that deals with the study of motion with the reference of mass and force is called dynamics. A body is said to be at rest if it does not change its position with respect to its surroundings. A body is said to be in motion if it changes its position with respect to its surroundings. Ifabody moves in an irregular manner, then its motion is called random motion. When each point of a body moves around a fixed point or axis, then the motion of this body is called rotatory motion. When a body moves to and fro about its mean position then this type of motion is knownas vibratory motion. * The location ofan object or a point ora place with respect to some reference point called origin is called its position. A bullet has a very small mass but its impact is so strong, when it is fired froma gun because of its very high speed. On the other hand, the impact of a loaded truck ona body coming in its way is very large even if the truck is moving slowly because of its large mass. Thus, one can conclude that 'quantity of motion' in an object depends on its mass and velocity. In terms of an equation, the momentum of an object is equal to the product of its mass and velocity. Momentum = Mass x Velocity p=mv (5.1) Momentum p is a vector quantity and its direction will be same as the direction of motion of object. An object at rest will have zero momentum because its velocity is zero. We can conclude from Eq. (5.1) that a moving object will have a large value of momentum if either its mass or its velocity or both have large values. The SI unit of momentum is kg ms". In daily life, we often face the situations where large momentum of the object is involved such as fast-moving train or an aefoplane. It is a common observation that ifa collision takes place, then a fast-moving vehicle is capable of causing more damage as compared with slow-moving identical vehicle. This is so because fast-moving vehicle has more momentum. You might be familiar with the sight of a road roller.

question: Explain Efficiency in Grade 9 Physics (Work, Energy and Power).
answer: The efficiency of working system is very important. The efficiency of a working system shows how much input energy is converted into useful output energy or work. The percentage efficiency of system is defined as under: % Efficiency = Useful energy output yg, Total energy input It can also be defined in terms of power i.e., % Efficiency = Useful power output | ggo, Total power input All machines have moving parts. A part of input energy is used to overcome the friction between these moving parts and this energy appears in the form of heat, sound etc. That is why the efficiency of a machine or any working system is always less than 100 % because of friction. If the efficiency is 50%, it means that only half of the input energy is given out as useful work and the rest is converted to heat due to friction. If we could build a system that operates without friction, then it would be 100 % efficient and all the input energy will be converted completely into useful work by the system. In practice, all machines have some friction in them and the output work is always less than the input work. Examples of machines include a lever, engine of an automobile, and perpetual motion machine Sample Problem

question: Explain Introduction in Grade 9 Physics (Particle Theory of Matter).
answer: Matter consists of extremely small particles called atoms, molecules or ions and these particles are not visible to naked eye. One or more atoms of same or different elements combine to form a molecule. Matter exists in three states i.e., solid, liquid and gas. Matter can change its state on heating or cooling. For example, ice (the solid form of water) will convert into liquid form ie., water on heating. Further heating of water will convert it into steam which is the gaseous form of water. Similarly, the gaseous form of water i.e., steam can be transformed into its liquid form on cooling. Further cooling will transform the water into its solid form ice. Pressure can also change the state of matter. Gases can be liquified under high pressure. The existence of matter i.e., solid, liquid and gas may be explained on the basis of the particle theory of matter.

question: Explain Particle Theory Of Matter in Grade 9 Physics (Particle Theory of Matter).
answer: The particle theory of matter is based on the following postulates. (a) Matter consists of extremely small particles. These particles are atoms, molecules or ions. (b) Particles are in constant motion and thus possess kinetic energy. The motion of particles can be translational, vibrational or rotational or a combination of these motions or all of these. The nature of motion of particles depends on the state of matter. (c) The particles of matter attract each other and this force depends on the separation between the particles. Smaller the separation between the particles, the greater will be the force of attraction between them.

question: Explain Physics of Solids in Grade 12 Physics.
answer: INTRODUCTION Basically, there are three states of matter solids, liquids and gas. The liquidand gas are compressible and have ability to flow, whereas, solids are incompressible and have definite volume and shapes. These are due to the closeness of their atoms or, molecules. Similarly, there are several kinds of solids, among these, each of them has its different characteristics and properties. Some solids are crystalline while others are amorphous or polymer, some are elastic while others are rigid, some are brittle while others are plastic or ductile, some have electrical conductivity while others have magnetic conductivity. For example, diamond is hard, lead is soft, steal is strong, glass is weak, copper has electrical conductivity and iron has magnetic conductivity. Many solids can be deformed in the form of change in their length, volume or shape by a deforming force. These deformations can be studied in terms of stress and strain.: In this unit we will explain classification of solids. For example, there are three classes of solids with respect to their structure, named as: crystalline, amorphous and polymer. Electrically, there are three classes of solids such as: insulators, conductors and semi-conductors, these can be studied using band theory of solids. Magnetically, the three types of solids are paramagnetic, diamagnetic and ferromagnetic. In addition to the magnetic classes, we will also discuss the phenomenon of hysteresis and hysteresis loop by magnetizing and demagnetizing the magnetic materials.

answer: An amplifier is an electronic circuit which converts.a small input A.C. signal into a large output A.C. signal under the action of a transistor. The amplification takes place under the following three configurations ie., common base amplifier, common emitter amplifier and common collector amplifier, but common emitter amplifier is used mostly. Consider the operation of a common emitter NPN transistor as shown in Fig.17.32. The emitter-base junction is forward biased by using a battery Vas and a resistor Rx called base or input resistor, whereas collector is reverse biased by using another battery Vcc through a resistor Rc known as collector or load resistor. The input A.C. signal is applied in the base and emitter section of the circuit. And the output signal is taken out from the collector-emitter section. In the absence of any input signal, the transistor is working in its normal mode. Now when an A.C. signal is applied at the input terminals of the circuit, then during the positive half cycle of the signal, the base of the transistor which acts as driven element becomes more Positive and it increases the forward biasing across the emitter-base junction. Therefore, more electrons flow from the emitter to the collector through the base and it causes of an increase collector current Ic by f times the input base current Ip (1, =B1, ). As a result, a greater voltage drops across the collector load resistance Rc due to the increased collector Ic. Thus, we have a large output half A.C.
